title: Dewey Decimal Classification: ten main classes that divide all knowledge by discipline
evidence: stated
status: settled
event_date: 2026-06-02
source: Melvil Dewey, A Classification and Subject Index for Cataloguing and Arranging the Books and Pamphlets of a Library (1876)
---

A library shelving scheme first published in 1876 that gives every book a number, so that books on the same subject stand next to each other.

## Ten classes, then tens, then decimals

Knowledge is split into ten main classes: 000 computer science and general works, 100 philosophy and psychology, 200 religion, 300 social sciences, 400 language, 500 science, 600 technology, 700 arts and recreation, 800 literature, 900 history and geography. Each class splits into ten divisions and each division into ten sections. After three digits a decimal point allows any depth: 641.5 is cooking, 641.815 is bread.

## The discipline decides, not the topic

A subject has no single home. Bread can sit under cooking (641), under customs around food (394) or under fermentation technology (660). The scheme asks which discipline a book is written from, and that decides its one place.

## Relative location

The number belongs to the subject, not to the shelf. When the collection grows, books move along the shelves but keep their numbers. Before Dewey, many libraries gave each book a fixed shelf position.

## What I said reading it

One book, one number, one place. Whatever a second subject would have wanted from the book is lost to that subject. Compare [[library-of-congress-classification]], which makes the same one-place choice with letters.
